name: Rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings (Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: An edge-colouring of a simple graph is proper when adjacent edges (edges sharing an endpoint, i.e. adjacent vertices of the line graph) receive distinct colours, and a cycle is rainbow when its edges have pairwise distinct colours. The average degree of a finite graph is 2|E|/|V|. Theorem 1.1 of 'Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings' asserts an absolute constant C > 0 such that every properly edge-coloured graph on n >= 3 vertices with average degree at least C * log n * log log n contains a rainbow cycle. The formalization states this as the log n * log log n instance of a parameterised threshold statement RainbowCycleThreshold f. The lower-bound constructions discussed in the paper have average degree Omega(log n) and no rainbow cycle, leaving a log log n gap to this upper bound. This problem shares its source paper with P014, which formalizes the paper's hypercube lemma; here the target is the main theorem.
formal_statement: theorem P045 : RainbowCycleThreshold.{u, v} (fun n => Real.log n * Real.log (Real.log n))

name: Clustered Hajós (Liu–Wood, Theorem 6)
msc: 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C83 Graph minors
informal_statement_summary: A vertex coloring (adjacent vertices may share a color) has clustering η when every connected monochromatic component has at most η vertices; a graph is clusteredly k-colorable with clustering η when such a coloring with k colors exists. A graph contains a subdivision of K_n when it has n distinct branch vertices joined, for each pair, by internally disjoint paths (the standard path model, formalized by nonempty simple vertex lists chained along edges). Hajós conjectured that graphs with no K_(s+1)-subdivision are properly s-colorable; Catlin disproved this for s ≥ 6. Theorem 6 of Liu and Wood, 'Clustered Variants of Hajós' Conjecture', rescues the conjecture in the clustered setting: for every s there is an η = η(s) such that every finite graph containing no subdivision of K_(s+1) admits a coloring with max(4s − 5, 1) colors and clustering η. The paper's proof relies on two companion papers and the Liu–Thomas structure theorem for graphs excluding a bounded-degree subdivision.
formal_statement: theorem P046 (s : ℕ) : ∃ η : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V), ¬ IsCliqueSubdivision G (s + 1) → ClusterColorable G (max (4 * s - 5) 1) η

name: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture (Kühn–Sauermann–Steiner–Wigderson, Theorem 1.3)
msc: 05C83 Graph minors; 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: An odd K_t minor of G is a system of t vertex-disjoint trees in G, each equipped with a proper 2-coloring, such that every two trees are joined by an edge of G whose endpoints receive matching colors in their respective trees. The odd Hadwiger conjecture (Gerards–Seymour, 1993) asserts that graphs with no odd K_t minor are properly (t−1)-colorable. Theorem 1.3 of Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson, 'Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture', refutes this in a strong multiplicative sense: for every δ > 0 and all sufficiently large t there is a graph with no odd K_t minor whose chromatic number is at least (3/2 − δ)t. The construction takes complements of pseudorandom triangle-free graphs, which have independence number 2 and hence chromatic number at least n/2, and shows via a stability analysis that odd clique minors in such graphs cannot exceed order about n/3.
formal_statement: theorem P047 : ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ t₀ : ℕ, ∀ t : ℕ, t₀ ≤ t → ∃ n : ℕ, ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), HasPaperChromaticLowerBound G δ t ∧ OddCliqueMinorFree G t

name: A hypergraph bandwidth theorem (Lang–Sanhueza-Matamala, Theorem 3.5)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: For a k-uniform hypergraph G, tight connectivity means no isolated vertices plus connectivity of the line graph on E(G) whose adjacency is overlap in exactly k−1 vertices; a component is an edge-maximal spanning tightly connected subhypergraph. A Hamilton framework for a family P of s-vertex t-graphs selects in each member a component with a perfect fractional matching (total weight n/t) and an aperiodic closed tight walk (order 1 mod t), consistently across members obtained by deleting distinct vertices from a common (s+1)-vertex graph (F1-F4 of Definition 3.1). The t-clique graph of G has as edges the t-sets all of whose k-subsets are edges. G s-robustly satisfies P when the s-uniform property graph, whose edges are the s-sets inducing a member of P, has minimum 2t-degree at least (1 − 1/s²)·C(n−2t, s−2t). Theorem 3.5 of Lang and Sanhueza-Matamala, 'A hypergraph bandwidth theorem', asserts: for all k, t, s there are c > 0 and n₀ such that every k-graph G on n ≥ n₀ vertices whose clique graph robustly satisfies a family admitting a Hamilton framework contains every n-vertex blow-up of the (t−k+1)-st power of a tight k-cycle with clusters of size at most (log log n)^c. This unifies and extends the known Dirac-type Hamiltonicity results for hypergraphs to the bandwidth setting.
formal_statement: theorem P048 (k t s : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) (hkt : k ≤ t) (hts : 2 * t ≤ s) : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} {W : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype W], ∀ (P : Set (Hypergraph (Fin s))) (G : Hypergraph V) (H : Hypergraph W), n₀ ≤ Fintype.card V → Fintype.card W = Fintype.card V → IsSpanning G → IsUniform k G → AdmitsHamiltonFramework t s P → RobustlySatisfies t s (cliqueGraph k t G) P → IsBlowUpOfCyclePower H k t c → Embeds H G

name: Counting perfect matchings in Dirac hypergraphs (Kwan–Safavi–Wang, Theorem 1.7)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C30 Enumeration in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: For 1 ≤ d < k, let m_d(k,n) be the minimum d-degree forcing a perfect matching in an n-vertex k-uniform hypergraph (n divisible by k), and let α_d(k) = lim m_d(k,n)/C(n−d,k−d) be the asymptotic Dirac threshold (the limit exists by Ferber–Kwan; its value is a major open problem for most d, k). A fractional perfect matching assigns weights in [0,1] to edges with unit sum at every vertex; its entropy is Σ x_e log(1/x_e), and h(G) is the supremum of these entropies. Theorem 1.7 of Kwan, Safavi and Wang, 'Counting Perfect Matchings in Dirac Hypergraphs', extends the Cuckler–Kahn theorem to hypergraphs: for fixed γ > 0, every family of k-graphs with minimum d-degree at least (α_d(k)+γ)C(n−d,k−d) has Φ(G) = e^{h(G)}(1/e + o(1))^{(1−1/k)n} perfect matchings. The formalization states the equivalent logarithmic form: the normalized error (log Φ(G) − h(G) + (1−1/k)n)/n tends to zero along every such family, indexed by n = km.
formal_statement: theorem P049 (d k : ℕ) (hd : 1 ≤ d) (hdk : d < k) (γ α : ℝ) (hγ : 0 < γ) (hα : IsAsymptoticDiracThreshold d k α) (G : (m : ℕ) → Hypergraph (Fin (k * m))) (hG : IsDiracFamily d k γ α G) : HasEntropyCountingAsymptotic k G

name: Dirac's theorem for linear hypergraphs (Im–Lee, Theorem 1.2)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C07 Vertex degrees
informal_statement_summary: A k-uniform hypergraph is linear when any two distinct edges share at most one vertex. Theorem 1.2 of Im and Lee, 'Dirac's theorem for linear hypergraphs', generalizes Dirac's theorem: for every ε > 0 and k ≥ 2 there are constants C and n₀ such that every n-vertex linear k-graph with n ≥ n₀ and minimum vertex degree at least n/k + C contains a matching covering at least (1−ε)n vertices. The case k = 2 follows from Dirac's theorem; the degree condition is asymptotically best possible by a construction from mutually orthogonal Latin squares (Proposition 1.3). The proof determines the perfect fractional matching threshold for linear hypergraphs via Farkas' lemma, then regularizes and applies the Pippenger–Spencer semirandom method.
formal_statement: theorem P050 (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) : ∃ C n₀ : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ 0 < n₀ ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, n₀ ≤ n → ∀ H : Hypergraph (Fin n), IsSpanning H → IsUniform k H → IsLinear H → (n : ℝ) / (k : ℝ) + (C : ℝ) ≤ (minimumVertexDegree H : ℝ) → HasAlmostPerfectMatching H ε

name: Helly number for agreeing orders of marked cliques (Biró–Lehel–Tóth, Theorem 1)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 06A05 Total orders; 52A35 Helly-type theorems
informal_statement_summary: A 2-extreme marked r-uniform clique on a vertex set V assigns to every r-subset (edge) a distinguished 2-element boundary set contained in it. A linear order (formalized by a rank function injective on the relevant subset) agrees with the marking on U ⊆ V when, for every edge inside U, the two boundary vertices are the minimum and maximum of the edge. Theorem 1 of Biró, Lehel and Tóth, 'Helly-type theorems for the ordering of the vertices of a hypergraph', is a Helly-type theorem: for r ≥ 3, a marked clique on at least 2r−2 vertices admits a globally agreeing linear order if and only if every subset of 2r−2 vertices does. The number 2r−2 is sharp. The case r = 3 is of particular interest in the axiomatic theory of betweenness. [Statement adopted 2026-09-08 from the vb/Folders formalisation: the conclusion now includes the sharpness clause HasSharpExample r, that some 2-extreme marked r-clique on 2r − 2 vertices has agreeing orders on all (2r − 3)-subsets but no global one.]
formal_statement: theorem P051 (r : ℕ) (hr : 3 ≤ r) : (∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V], 2 * r - 2 ≤ Fintype.card V → ∀ H : TwoExtremeMarkedClique V r, H.HasAgreeingOrderOn Finset.univ ↔ H.HasLocalAgreeingOrders (2 * r - 2)) ∧ HasSharpExample r

name: Distinct clique sizes in uniform hypergraphs (Gao, Theorem 1.1; Erdős problem #775)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C69 Vertex subsets with special properties; 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: In a k-uniform hypergraph, a complete set is a vertex set all of whose k-subsets are edges, and a clique is an inclusion-maximal complete set. Theorem 1.1 of Jun Gao, 'On cliques in hypergraphs', shows that for every k ≥ 3 and every constant C there is N(k,C) such that every n-vertex k-uniform hypergraph with n ≥ N has at most n − C distinct clique sizes — equivalently, the maximal possible deficit f(n,k) = n − g(n,k) tends to infinity. The 3-uniform case answers a question of Erdős (problem #775). For graphs (k = 2) the story goes back to Moon–Moser (1965), and Erdős's construction shows f(n,3) ≤ log* n, so the growth of the deficit is genuinely slow. The proof orders maximal cliques by size and builds a (k−1,C)-layered rooted tree whose order is bounded in terms of k and C alone.
formal_statement: theorem P052 (k C : ℕ) (hk : 3 ≤ k) : ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → ∀ H : Hypergraph (Fin n), IsSpanning H → IsUniform k H → distinctCliqueSizeCount k H ≤ n - C

name: Hypergraph joints (Chao–Yu, Theorem 1.12)
msc: 52C35 Arrangements of points, flats, hyperplanes; 05D99 Extremal combinatorics; 51A20 Configuration theorems in linear incidence geometry
informal_statement_summary: Fix a multihypergraph H on [d] with edges colored by [r] so that color i consists of distinct edges of cardinality d − k_i (1 ≤ k_i ≤ d−1). Given, for each color, a finite indexed family of k_i-dimensional affine flats in F^d, a point p is an H-joint if flats can be selected, one per edge, together with an invertible affine map A with A(0) = p, such that each selected flat is the A-image of the coordinate subspace complementary to its edge. Theorem 1.12 of Chao and Yu, 'When Joints Meet Extremal Graph Theory: Hypergraph Joints', bounds the number of H-joints by C_{H,w}·|F₁|^{w̄₁}⋯|F_r|^{w̄_r} for every fractional cover w of H, with the explicit constant C_{H,w} = d!^{|w|−1}·∏_i (1/k_i!)^{w̄_i}·∏_e (w(e)/w̄_{c(e)})^{w(e)}. The classical joints theorem (Guth–Katz type, sharp constant, over every field) is the one-color instance; the theorem also yields the partial shadow phenomenon of Bollobás–Eccles via projected configurations.
formal_statement: theorem P053 {d r : ℕ} (H : ColoredMultiHypergraph d r) (k : Fin r → ℕ) (hk : ∀ i, 1 ≤ k i ∧ k i ≤ d - 1) (hUniform : IsUniformlyColored H k) (w : Fin H.edgeCount → ℝ) (hw : WeightCovers H w) (𝔽 : Type*) [Field 𝔽] (C : HJointConfiguration d r H 𝔽 k) : (C.joints.card : ℝ) ≤ jointConstant H k w * flatFamilyProduct C w

name: Cycle Double Cover Conjecture
msc: 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C40 Connectivity; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: A finite multigraph may have loops and parallel edges. An edge is a bridge if deleting it separates its two endpoints, and the graph is bridgeless when it has no bridge. A cycle is a nonempty inclusion-minimal edge set having even degree at every vertex; thus a loop is a one-edge cycle and two parallel edges can form a two-edge cycle. A cycle double cover is a finite multiset of cycles, represented by a list so repetitions are retained, in which every edge occurs exactly twice. The cycle double cover conjecture asserts that every finite bridgeless multigraph has a cycle double cover.
formal_statement: theorem P054 {V : Type u} {E : Type v} [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] [Finite V] [Fintype E] (G : Multigraph V E) (hG : G.Bridgeless) : Nonempty G.CycleDoubleCover

name: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: The graph is the same finite multigraph used by the cycle double cover problem. It is assumed simple, its underlying simple graph is regular of degree three, and it is 2-connected in the shared vertex-connectivity sense (SimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 2: more than two vertices, and still connected after deleting any one vertex). A circuit reuses the existing definition of a cycle as a nonempty inclusion-minimal even edge set. A circuit double cover is represented canonically by assigning multiplicity zero, one, or two to every circuit so that every edge has total multiplicity exactly two; this avoids counting orderings of the same family as different covers. Every properly 3-edge-coloured graph satisfying these hypotheses on n vertices has at least 2^(n/2 - 1) circuit double covers.
formal_statement: theorem P055 {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (G : Multigraph V E) (hSimple : G.IsSimple) (hCubic : G.toSimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree 3) (hG : G.toSimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 2) (c : G.ProperThreeEdgeColoring) : 2 ^ (Fintype.card V / 2 - 1) ≤ G.circuitDoubleCovers.card

name: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers at High Girth
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C40 Connectivity; 05C21 Flows in graphs
informal_statement_summary: The graph is the same finite multigraph used by the cycle double cover problem, with circuit double covers recorded canonically by cycle multiplicities. Here the graph is simple, cubic, and 3-connected in the shared vertex-connectivity sense (SimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 3: more than three vertices, and still connected after deleting any two), and has girth at least 16: every cycle, in the inclusion-minimal even edge set sense, has at least sixteen edges. Theorem 1.8 of Hušek and Šámal, 'Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers', asserts a uniform exponential rate: there is c > 0 and a threshold n₀ such that every such graph on n ≥ n₀ vertices has at least 2^(cn) circuit double covers. Unlike Theorem 1.7 (Problem 55), no 3-edge-colorability is assumed, so the result covers high-girth snarks — historically the presumed hard case of the cycle double cover conjecture. The threshold 16 comes from the margin 16 > 6·log₂6 ≈ 15.51.
formal_statement: theorem P056 : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} {E : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (G : Multigraph V E), G.IsSimple → G.toSimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree 3 → G.toSimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 3 → G.HasGirthAtLeast 16 → n₀ ≤ Fintype.card V → (2 : ℝ) ^ (c * Fintype.card V) ≤ G.circuitDoubleCovers.card

name: Divisorial Gonality of Finite Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: A divisor is an integer-valued chip configuration on the vertices of a finite loopless multigraph. Firing a vertex sends one chip along each incident edge, and two divisors are linearly equivalent when their difference is generated by such firings. Every connected multigraph of cycle rank g = |E|-|V|+1 is conjectured to have an effective divisor D of degree at most floor((g+3)/2) whose firing class can place a chip at every prescribed vertex: for each q there is an effective E linearly equivalent to D with E(q) at least one. This is Baker's divisorial gonality conjecture. It is known through genus five and open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P057 (G : CFGraph) (_hConnected : graph_connected G) : ∃ D : CFDiv G, effective D ∧ deg D ≤ (genus G + 3) / 2 ∧ ∀ q : G.V, ∃ E : CFDiv G, effective E ∧ linear_equiv G D E ∧ 1 ≤ E q

name: Brill--Noether Existence for Finite Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: For a connected finite loopless multigraph G, divisors are integer-valued chip configurations modulo chip-firing. A divisor has rank at least r when removing every effective divisor of degree r leaves a firing class containing an effective representative, and it has rank exactly r when this holds for r but not r+1. Given nonnegative integers r and d, let rho(g,r,d) = g - (r+1)(g-d+r), where g = |E(G)|-|V(G)|+1. Baker's Brill--Noether existence conjecture asserts that rho at least zero guarantees a divisor of rank exactly r and degree at most d on every such graph. The conjecture is known for genus at most five and open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P058 (G : CFGraph) (_hConnected : graph_connected G) (r d : ℤ) (_hr : 0 ≤ r) (_hd : 0 ≤ d) (_hρ : 0 ≤ brillNoetherNumber (genus G) r d) : ∃ D : CFDiv G, divisorRankEq G D r ∧ deg D ≤ d

name: Combinatorial Brill--Noether Existence for Metric Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: A metric graph is represented by a connected finite loopless multigraph whose edge occurrences have positive real lengths. Its points include both vertices and all interior points of the edge intervals. Divisors are finitely supported integer-valued functions on these points, and linear equivalence is generated by divisors of continuous piecewise-affine functions with integral slopes. Given nonnegative integers r and d, let rho(g,r,d) = g - (r+1)(g-d+r). Baker's metric-graph Brill--Noether theorem says that rho at least zero guarantees a divisor of rank exactly r and degree at most d on every metric graph of genus g. Baker's proof passes through classical algebraic Brill--Noether theory, the specialization lemma, and a semicontinuity argument. The challenge is to find a purely combinatorial proof of the same theorem.
formal_statement: theorem P059 (G : MetricGraph) (_hConnected : G.Connected) (r d : ℤ) (_hr : 0 ≤ r) (_hd : 0 ≤ d) (_hρ : 0 ≤ brillNoetherNumber G.genus r d) : ∃ D : MetricDiv G, metricDivisorRankEq G D r ∧ metricDegree D ≤ d

name: Chvátal's Toughness Conjecture
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: The toughness of a finite graph measures how sturdily it is connected: G is t-tough when every vertex set whose deletion disconnects the graph contains at least t vertices per component created (formalized with real t via the component count of the induced graph on the complement). Chvátal's conjecture (1973) asserts that some fixed toughness forces Hamiltonicity: there is t > 0 such that every t-tough graph on at least three vertices has a Hamiltonian cycle. Chvátal's original candidate t = 2 was refuted by Bauer, Broersma and Veldman (2000), who constructed (9/4 − ε)-tough non-Hamiltonian graphs, so any witness satisfies t ≥ 9/4; the conjecture remains open, with t = 3 a natural candidate.
formal_statement: theorem P060 : ∃ t : ℝ, 0 < t ∧ ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V), 3 ≤ Fintype.card V → G.IsTough t → G.IsHamiltonian

name: Seymour's Exact Edge-Colouring Conjecture for Planar Multigraphs
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C10 Planar graphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties
informal_statement_summary: For a loopless multigraph, the degree of a vertex is its number of incident edges, an edge crosses a vertex set when it has one endpoint on each side, and the graph is oddly d-edge-connected when every proper vertex set of odd size is crossed by at least d edges. Planarity is read through the underlying simple graph (parallel edges and loops never obstruct an embedding) using the rotation-system genus-zero characterization of the shared library. Seymour's exact conjecture (1970s) asserts that every d-regular oddly d-edge-connected planar loopless multigraph is d-edge-colourable: its edges can be coloured with d colours so that edges sharing a vertex differ. The case d = 3 is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem (Tait); d = 4, 5 are due to Guenin, d = 6 to Dvořák–Kawarabayashi–Král', and d = 7, 8 to Chudnovsky–Edwards–Kawarabayashi–Seymour. The conjecture is open for every d ≥ 9; without planarity the Petersen graph refutes the statement already at d = 3.
formal_statement: theorem P061 : ∀ (d : ℕ) (V : Type u) (E : Type v) [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (M : Multigraph V E), (∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) → M.IsRegular d → M.OddlyEdgeConnected d → M.IsPlanar → M.EdgeColorable d

name: Tutte's 5-Flow Conjecture
msc: 05C21 Flows in graphs; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A nowhere-zero flow on a multigraph assigns a nonzero group value to every edge, in a fixed representative orientation of each edge, so that Kirchhoff's law holds at every vertex; reorienting an edge negates its value, so the orientation choice is immaterial, and loops enter both sides of the law and are unconstrained. Tutte's 5-flow conjecture (1954) asserts that every bridgeless multigraph has a nowhere-zero flow with values in ZMod 5 (by Tutte's theorem only the order of the group matters, so this is equivalent to the classical integer formulation with values of absolute value below five). Jaeger proved the 8-flow theorem and Seymour the 6-flow theorem; five would be best possible, since the Petersen graph has no nowhere-zero 4-flow. For planar graphs the conjecture is the dual of the Five Colour Theorem. A minimal counterexample is, by Kochol's reductions, a cyclically 6-edge-connected snark of girth at least eleven.
formal_statement: theorem P062 : ∀ (V : Type u) (E : Type v) [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (M : Multigraph V E), M.Bridgeless → ∃ f : E → ZMod 5, M.IsNowhereZeroFlow f

name: Mader's Connectivity Conjecture
msc: 05C40 Connectivity; 05C35 Extremal problems in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: The average degree of a finite simple graph is the sum of its vertex degrees divided by the number of vertices (equivalently twice the edge count over the vertex count). Mader conjectured in 1979 that every graph of average degree at least 3k-1 contains a (k+1)-connected subgraph; the subgraph may be taken induced, since adding edges preserves vertex connectivity. The conjecture has been open for almost half a century: Mader proved in 1972 that average degree 4k-2 suffices, the known sufficient linear factor was improved over the years but never reached 3, and Krone proved the minimum-degree analogue (minimum degree 3k-1 forces a (k+1)-connected subgraph on more than 2k vertices). If true, the bound 3k-1 is sharp for every value of the core connectivity.
formal_statement: theorem P063 : ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (k : ℕ), 1 ≤ k → (3 * k - 1 : ℚ) ≤ G.averageDegree → ∃ s : Set V, (G.induce s).IsVertexConnected (k + 1)

name: The Berge–Fulkerson Conjecture
msc: 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties (factorization, matching); 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A perfect matching of a multigraph is an edge set meeting every vertex in exactly one edge. The Berge-Fulkerson conjecture (Fulkerson 1971) asserts that every bridgeless cubic multigraph has six perfect matchings that together cover every edge exactly twice - equivalently, doubling every edge yields a 6-edge-colourable multigraph. For 3-edge-colourable cubic graphs the six matchings are the three colour classes taken twice, so any counterexample is a snark; the Petersen graph and all verified snark families satisfy the conjecture. By Mazzuoccolo's theorem it is equivalent to Berge's conjecture that five perfect matchings suffice to cover every edge at least once, and it implies the Fan-Raspaud conjecture that three perfect matchings can avoid a common edge.
formal_statement: theorem P064 : ∀ (V : Type u) (E : Type v) [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (M : Multigraph V E), (∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) → M.IsRegular 3 → M.Bridgeless → ∃ P : Fin 6 → Finset E, (∀ i, M.IsPerfectMatchingSet (P i)) ∧ ∀ e : E, (Finset.univ.filter fun i => e ∈ P i).card = 2

name: The Kahn--Kalai Counterexample to Borsuk's Conjecture
msc: 52A20 Convex sets in n dimensions; 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: Borsuk conjectured that every bounded set in d-dimensional Euclidean space can be covered by d+1 subsets of strictly smaller diameter. Kahn and Kalai disproved this in 1993 using the Frankl--Wilson intersection theorem. Their construction on balanced bipartitions of a 52-element set gives a finite set in an affine space of dimension 1325 such that every colouring with 1326 colours has a monochromatic pair at the full diameter. Thus the colour classes cannot all have smaller diameter. The formal statement uses this concrete finite counterexample; finiteness also makes the set automatically bounded. The corrected count has half of C(52,26) points, while a diameter-avoiding subfamily has at most C(51,12) points, so in fact the construction needs at least 1562 smaller-diameter parts.
formal_statement: theorem P065 : ∃ S : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325)), 0 < Metric.diam (S : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325))) ∧ ∀ c : S → Fin 1326, ∃ x y : S, c x = c y ∧ dist x y = Metric.diam (S : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325)))

name: The Tangle-Decider Conjecture
msc: 05C40 Connectivity; 05C83 Graph minors; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: An oriented separation of a finite simple graph is a pair (A,B) of vertex sets covering the graph, with no edge between A\B and B\A; its order is |A intersect B|. A k-tangle in Diestel's sense chooses exactly one orientation of every separation of order below k, and no three (not necessarily distinct) chosen small sides induce subgraphs whose union is the whole graph. The tangle-decider conjecture asks whether every such tangle is induced by majority vote by a vertex set X: for every chosen (A,B), |X intersect A| < |X intersect B|. The conjecture is known for k at most 3 and remains open for k at least 4. Every tangle does have an integral weighted decider, and a 2024 finite-reduction theorem reduces each fixed order to connected graphs of size bounded solely in k.
formal_statement: theorem P066 : ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (τ : G.Tangle k), ∃ X : Finset V, τ.IsDecidedBy X

name: Carmesin–Lichev: Embedding Homologically Trivial Two-Complexes in Exponential Time
msc: 57Q35 Embeddings and immersions; 57M15 Relations with graph theory; 68Q25 Analysis of algorithms and problem complexity; 55N35 Homology and cohomology theories
informal_statement_summary: A finite two-dimensional simplicial complex is given by numbered vertices together with its edges and triangles. Its integral first homology is trivial when every integral 1-cycle is the boundary of an integral 2-chain. The problem asks for a deterministic algorithm that decides in time 2^(n^c), for some constant c, which such complexes embed topologically in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Embeddability of arbitrary finite 2-complexes in R^3 is decidable and NP-hard. Carmesin and Lichev observe that, by Carmesin's characterizations, embeddability of 2-complexes with trivial rational first homology is polynomially equivalent to 3-sphere recognition, which lies in NP by Ivanov and Schleimer; this gives the exponential bound, while polynomial time remains open. The formalization uses a canonical barycentric realization, explicit integral boundary matrices, a fixed binary encoding, and Mathlib's deterministic Turing-machine runtime model.
formal_statement: theorem P067 : ∃ c, EmbeddabilityInTime fun n ↦ 2 ^ n ^ c

name: Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture
msc: 05C10 Planar graphs; geometric and topological aspects; 05C83 Graph minors; 57M15 Relations with graph theory
informal_statement_summary: A finite planar cover of a graph is a finite planar graph equipped with a surjective graph homomorphism that maps the neighborhood of every covering vertex bijectively onto the neighborhood of its image. Negami's planar-cover conjecture says that a connected graph has such a cover exactly when it embeds in the projective plane. Work on the excluded minors for the projective plane reduces the entire open direction to one graph: the complete multipartite graph K_{1,2,2,2}, equivalently an octahedral graph joined to one apex. The problem asserts that this graph has no finite planar cover. Recent work rules out every cover with fewer than fourteen sheets and imposes strong connectivity constraints on any minimal counterexample, but the unrestricted statement remains open. The formalization defines graph covers directly and expresses planarity through finite planar rotation systems.
formal_statement: theorem P068 : ¬ K1222.HasFinitePlanarCover

name: Algebraic Connectivity of Token Graphs
msc: 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 60J27 Continuous-time Markov processes on discrete state spaces
informal_statement_summary: For a finite graph G on n vertices, the k-token graph has the k-element subsets of the vertex set as its vertices; two configurations are adjacent when one token moves along an edge of G to an unoccupied vertex. Algebraic connectivity is the second-smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian, counted with multiplicity. The theorem states that for every 1 ≤ k < n, the algebraic connectivity of the k-token graph equals that of G. This was originally conjectured in the token-graph literature but is already a consequence of Caputo, Liggett and Richthammer's proof of Aldous' spectral-gap conjecture; the open question is to find a purely combinatorial or algebraic proof. The Lean statement works for disconnected graphs as well and uses Mathlib's ordered Hermitian eigenvalues, so zero eigenvalue multiplicities are represented faithfully.
formal_statement: theorem P069 (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (hk₀ : 1 ≤ k) (hkV : k < Fintype.card V) : algebraicConnectivity (tokenGraph G k) = algebraicConnectivity G

name: Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis
msc: 03E35 Consistency and independence results; 03E50 Continuum hypothesis and Martin's axiom
informal_statement_summary: First-order ZFC is deep-embedded in Lean: the language has a single binary membership relation, the eight core axioms and the separation and replacement schemas are spelled out as de Bruijn sentences, and CH is the sentence that every subset of P(omega) injects into omega or receives an injection from P(omega). The problem is three-optioned - prove CH from ZFC, refute it, or prove independence - and exactly one option is provable: the futility certificate. It is unconditional, since Lean's universes provide models of the embedded ZFC; a kernel-checked proof of either other option would witness an inconsistency of Lean itself. Goedel (1938) and Cohen (1963) supply the two model constructions, and the Flypitch project (Han-van Doorn, CPP 2020) formalized exactly this independence in Lean 3, so the problem is solved-in-principle at research level. Consequence is semantic (Mathlib has no syntactic calculus), which agrees with provability by Goedel completeness.
formal_statement: theorem P070 : Independent ZFC CH

name: Bipartite Unique-Neighbour Expanders via Ramanujan Graphs
msc: 05C48 Expander graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A bipartite graph is presented by the neighbourhood function of its left side. A right vertex is a unique neighbour of a set S of left vertices if it is adjacent to exactly one member of S, and a (c,d)-biregular unique-neighbour expander family is a uniform threshold delta > 0 together with (c,d)-biregular graphs of arbitrarily large order in which every nonempty set of at most delta|L| left vertices has a unique neighbour. Asherov and Dinur (2023) prove that there is a threshold function q-hat such that for every integer c0 > 5, real alpha > 1 and prime power q > q-hat(c0, alpha) with alpha c0 (q+1) an integer, there is a (c0(q+1), alpha c0 (q+1))-biregular unique-neighbour expander family - arbitrarily unbalanced sides - constructed in polynomial time by composing (q+1, q^3+1)-biregular Ramanujan graphs with a fixed-size gadget through a routed product. The formal statement records the mathematical existence with the paper's degree parameters; explicitness is not captured. Known true at research level: the paper's route needs a new average-degree bound for bipartite Ramanujan graphs, and the non-constructive route needs random biregular graph expansion. (Formalisation upgraded 2026-09-07: the challenge file now defines bipartite multigraphs, the routed product and Lemma 12 itself; the previous thin statement is kept in the attic.)
formal_statement: theorem P071 : ∃ qhat : ℕ → ℝ → ℕ, ∀ c₀ : ℕ, 5 < c₀ → ∀ α : ℝ, 1 < α → ∀ q : ℕ, IsPrimePow q → qhat c₀ α < q → ∀ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) = α * ((c₀ : ℝ) * ((q : ℝ) + 1)) → ∃ G : ℕ → BipartiteMultigraph, IsUniqueNeighbourExpanderFamily G (c₀ * (q + 1)) d

name: The Anonymous Lower Bound for Superpermutations
msc: 05A05 Permutations, words, matrices; 68R15 Combinatorics on words
informal_statement_summary: A superpermutation on n symbols is a word over an n-letter alphabet containing every permutation of the alphabet as a contiguous factor. In 2011 an anonymous poster on 4chan proved that every superpermutation on n symbols has length at least n! + (n-1)! + (n-2)! + n - 3, improving the Ashlock-Tillotson bound n! + (n-1)! + n - 2; the proof was written up by Houston, Pantone and Vatter in 2018. The bound is tight for n <= 4 (minimal lengths 1, 3, 9, 33) and off by one for n = 5 (minimum 153). The proof counts wasted letters: a letter is wasted unless it completes the first occurrence of a permutation; the first n-1 letters are wasted, each of the (n-1)! cyclic classes of permutations forces a wasted letter upon completion, and each of the (n-2)! trajectories - chains of n-1 cyclic classes linked by single wasted letters - forces a further, distinct wasted letter to change trajectory. The formal statement needs no hypothesis on n, natural-number arithmetic making the small cases trivial. Known true; the combinatorial proof has not been formalized.
formal_statement: theorem P072 : ∀ (n : ℕ) (w : List (Fin n)), IsSuperpermutation n w → n ! + (n - 1)! + (n - 2)! + n - 3 ≤ w.length

name: The Alon–Tarsi Conjecture
msc: 05B15 Orthogonal arrays, Latin squares, Room squares; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A Latin square of order n is an n-by-n array of n symbols with no repeated symbol in any row or column; its sign is the product of the signs of its n row permutations and n column permutations, and it is even or odd accordingly. The Alon-Tarsi conjecture (1992) asserts that for every even n the numbers of even and odd Latin squares of order n differ. For odd n >= 3 the two numbers are equal, since swapping two rows is a sign-reversing involution. The conjecture is known for n = p+1 (Drisko 1997) and n = p-1 (Glynn 2010) with p an odd prime, hence for every even n <= 24; the smallest open case is n = 26. By Huang and Rota it implies Rota's basis conjecture in even dimension over characteristic zero, and via the Alon-Tarsi polynomial method it implies the Dinitz conjecture for even n. The signed count is usually computed over row-reduced squares (first row in natural order), which for even n differs from the full signed count by the factor n!.
formal_statement: theorem P073 : ∀ n : ℕ, Even n → (Finset.univ.filter fun L : LatinSquare n => L.sign = 1).card ≠ (Finset.univ.filter fun L : LatinSquare n => L.sign = -1).card

name: The Collatz Conjecture
msc: 11B37 Recurrences; 37P99 Arithmetic and non-Archimedean dynamical systems
informal_statement_summary: The Collatz map sends an even number n to n/2 and an odd n to 3n+1. The Collatz conjecture (1937) asserts that iterating this map from any positive integer eventually reaches 1. It has been verified for all n < 2^68 (Barina 2020); Tao (2019) proved that almost all orbits attain almost bounded values; and any nontrivial cycle would have length at least 17,087,915 (Eliahou 1993, since improved). The conjecture is equivalent to the conjunction of two statements: no orbit diverges, and the only cycle is 1 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1; the sandwich formalizes this equivalence in both directions.
formal_statement: theorem P074 : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → CollatzReachesOne n

name: Bounded Avoidability Index of Patterns
msc: 68R15 Combinatorics on words; 05D10 Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: A pattern is a word over variables; it occurs in a word when a non-erasing substitution of the variables by nonempty words turns it into a factor. A pattern is k-avoidable if some infinite word over k letters contains no occurrence of it, and avoidable if it is k-avoidable for some k (Zimin's theorem characterises the avoidable patterns). Currie asked at WORDS 2003 whether there is a pattern that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable, equivalently whether every avoidable pattern is 5-avoidable. Every avoidable binary pattern is 3-avoidable (Cassaigne, Roth), every doubled pattern is 3-avoidable (Ochem 2016), and Clark exhibited a pattern of avoidability index exactly 5, so 5 cannot be lowered; whether the index is bounded at all is open. The challenge asserts the affirmative answer.
formal_statement: theorem P075 : ∀ (m : ℕ) (p : List (Fin m)), IsAvoidable p → IsKAvoidable p 5

name: Conway's 99-Graph Problem
msc: 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A strongly regular graph with parameters (v, k, lambda, mu) is a k-regular graph on v vertices in which adjacent vertices have exactly lambda common neighbours and non-adjacent vertices exactly mu. Conway's 99-graph problem asks whether a strongly regular graph with parameters (99, 14, 1, 2) exists; Conway offered $1000 for a resolution. The parameters pass every known feasibility condition (eigenvalues 3 and -4 with multiplicities 54 and 44, the Krein and absolute bounds); each vertex neighbourhood would be a perfect matching on 14 vertices, so every edge lies in a unique triangle; the sibling parameter sets (9, 4, 1, 2) and (243, 22, 1, 2) are realised by the Paley graph on nine vertices and the Berlekamp-van Lint-Seidel graph. Strong restrictions on the automorphism group of a hypothetical graph are known (Makhnev-Minakova). The problem is open in both directions; a positive answer is equivalent to a symmetric 0/1 matrix A of order 99 with zero diagonal and A^2 = 14I + A + 2(J - I - A), which a computer search could certify.
formal_statement: theorem P076 : ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 99)) (_ : DecidableRel G.Adj), G.IsSRGWith 99 14 1 2

name: The 57-regular Moore Graph
msc: 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs; 05C12 Distance in graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A Moore graph of degree k and diameter 2 is a k-regular graph of diameter 2 and girth 5; it has k^2 + 1 vertices and is strongly regular with parameters (k^2 + 1, k, 0, 1). Hoffman and Singleton proved that such graphs exist only for k in {2, 3, 7, 57}, and the first three cases are realised by the pentagon, the Petersen graph and the Hoffman-Singleton graph. The problem asks whether the last case exists: is there a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1), i.e. a 57-regular graph of diameter 2 and girth 5 on 3250 vertices? It is open.
formal_statement: theorem P077 : ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)) (_ : DecidableRel G.Adj), G.IsSRGWith 3250 57 0 1

name: The Borodin–Kostochka Conjecture
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C07 Vertex degrees
informal_statement_summary: For a finite simple graph G let chi(G) be the chromatic number, Delta(G) the maximum degree and omega(G) the clique number. Brooks' theorem gives chi(G) <= max(Delta(G), omega(G)) for Delta(G) >= 3. The Borodin-Kostochka conjecture (1977) states that every finite simple graph with maximum degree at least 9 satisfies chi(G) <= max(Delta(G) - 1, omega(G)); equivalently, every graph with Delta >= 9 and omega < Delta is (Delta - 1)-colourable. The threshold 9 is sharp (Catlin graphs). Reed proved the conjecture for Delta >= 10^14, and it is open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P078 : ∀ {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj], 9 ≤ G.maxDegree → G.chromaticNumber ≤ max (G.maxDegree - 1) G.cliqueNum

name: Antipodal Edge-Colourings of the Hypercube
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C38 Paths and cycles
informal_statement_summary: Let d >= 2 and two-colour the edges of the d-dimensional hypercube Q_d so that antipodal edges (an edge and its image under complementing every coordinate) receive opposite colours; no properness is imposed. Norine's conjecture states that some pair of antipodal vertices is then joined by a monochromatic path. The stronger conjecture that every two-colouring of Q_d admits an antipodal path with at most one colour change implies it. Open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P079 : ∀ (d : ℕ), 2 ≤ d → ∀ c : Sym2 (Q d) → Bool, IsAntipodalColoring d c → ∃ (x : Q d) (w : (H d).Walk x (antipode x)) (b : Bool), IsMonochromatic c w b

name: The Reconstruction Conjecture
msc: 05C60 Isomorphism problems (reconstruction conjecture, etc.)
informal_statement_summary: The card of a finite simple graph G at a vertex v is the vertex-deleted subgraph G - v. Two graphs have the same deck when a bijection sigma between their vertex sets pairs every card G - v with an isomorphic card G' - sigma(v), multiplicities retained and the card isomorphisms independent of each other. The Kelly-Ulam reconstruction conjecture states that two finite simple graphs on at least three vertices with the same deck are isomorphic. Known for disconnected graphs, trees, regular graphs and many other classes, and reducible to 2-connected graphs (Yang); open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P080 : ∀ {V : Type u} {V' : Type v} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (G' : SimpleGraph V'), 3 ≤ Fintype.card V → G.SameDeck G' → Nonempty (G ≃g G')

name: Lovász's Hamiltonian-Path Question for Vertex-Transitive Graphs
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields, etc.)
informal_statement_summary: A finite simple graph is vertex-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on the vertices. Lovász asked (1969) whether every finite connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path, a path visiting every vertex exactly once. The Hamiltonian-cycle version fails for exactly five known graphs (K_2, Petersen, Coxeter and their truncations), all of which have Hamiltonian paths. Open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P081 : ∀ {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), G.Connected → VertexTransitive G → ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.IsPath ∧ p.length + 1 = Fintype.card V

name: Graham's Graph-Pebbling Product Conjecture
msc: 05C76 Graph operations; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: A pebbling configuration assigns a nonnegative integer to each vertex of a graph. A legal move removes two pebbles from one vertex and adds one to an adjacent vertex. The pebbling number π(G) is the least n such that every configuration of n pebbles can place a pebble at any prescribed root using finitely many legal moves. Graham's conjecture asserts π(G □ H) ≤ π(G)π(H) for all finite connected simple graphs G and H, where □ is the Cartesian product. The formalization proves that the threshold exists and that requiring exactly n or at least n pebbles gives the same definition. The conjecture is open; the companion DISPROVE file asks for finite connected factors violating the inequality.
formal_statement: theorem P082 : ∀ {V : Type u} {W : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype W] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W), G.Connected → H.Connected → pebblingNumber (G □ H) ≤ pebblingNumber G * pebblingNumber H

name: Pebbling Number of a Path
msc: 05C05 Trees; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: A legal pebbling move removes two pebbles from a vertex and places one at an adjacent vertex. The pebbling number is the least size for which every configuration can reach every prescribed root by finitely many legal moves. For the path on n + 1 vertices, this number is exactly 2^n, for all n ≥ 0. This classical solved problem is an elementary calibration task reusing P082's definitions. A complete Lean solution is supplied, including arbitrary roots and the one-vertex case.
formal_statement: theorem P083 (n : ℕ) : pebblingNumber (pathGraph (n + 1)) = 2 ^ n

name: Cayley's Formula via Prüfer Codes
msc: 05C05 Trees; 05A19 Combinatorial identities, bijective combinatorics
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 84: Cayley's Formula via Prüfer Codes}
\refstepcounter{section}

Let $\mathcal{T}_n$ be the set of simple connected acyclic graphs on the fixed vertex set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. These are unrooted labelled trees: labels are distinguished, and we do not identify isomorphic graphs.

\begin{theorem}[Cayley's formula]
For $n\geq2$, $|\mathcal{T}_n|=n^{n-2}$. There is exactly one tree on a single vertex.
\end{theorem}

The formal statement combines the two cases as $|\mathcal{T}_n|=n^{n-2}$ for $n\geq1$, using natural subtraction, so its right side at $n=1$ is $1^0=1$.

The complete solution uses Prüfer codes, sequences of length $n-2$ with entries in the vertex set. Repeatedly delete the least-labelled leaf and record its unique neighbour until two vertices remain. The decoder joins the least remaining label absent from the current code to the first entry, removes that label and entry, and finally joins the two remaining labels. The two procedures are inverse, giving
\[
\mathcal{T}_n\simeq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^{\{0,\ldots,n-3\}}.
\]
The exponent set here has size $n-2$ and is empty when $n=2$.

See \cite{GraphTheoryNotesPrufer}. The private Lean solution adapts the Apache-2.0 ProofAtlas formalization \cite{ProofAtlas2026Cayley}, with source attribution, compatibility repairs and proof simplifications. It retains the actual encoder and decoder, not an arbitrary equivalence extracted from a cardinality theorem.

\begin{thebibliography}{2}
\bibitem{GraphTheoryNotesPrufer} \emph{Graph Theory Notes}, Section 3.1: Prüfer Codes. \url{https://ptwiddle.github.io/Graph-Theory-Notes/s_graphalgorithms_prufer.html}.
\bibitem{ProofAtlas2026Cayley} Advameg, Inc. \emph{Cayley's Formula for Labeled Trees: Lean Formalization}. ProofAtlas (2026). \url{https://www.proofatlas.ai/sources/cayley-tree-formula/}.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: For n ≥ 2, there are exactly n^(n-2) unrooted labelled trees on the fixed vertex set {0,…,n-1}; for n = 1 there is one. Trees are finite simple connected acyclic graphs, not graph-isomorphism classes. The complete solution constructs the classical Prüfer encoding, proves its decoder is inverse, and counts the length-n-2 codes. It is an elementary solved calibration problem. The public statement uses only mathlib's SimpleGraph.IsTree and Nat.card; all encoding and solution machinery is private.
formal_statement: theorem P084 (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) : Nat.card {G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) // G.IsTree} = n ^ (n - 2)

name: Lonely Runner Conjecture (Integer Speeds)
msc: 11K60 Diophantine approximation; 11J13 Simultaneous homogeneous approximation, linear forms
informal_statement_summary: For any k ≥ 1 nonzero integer speeds v₁,…,v_k, there is a real time t such that every t vᵢ is at distance at least 1/(k+1) from the nearest integer. This is the stationary-runner integer formulation: k speeds correspond to k+1 runners. Negative and repeated speeds are allowed. The full conjecture remains open; recent preprints report computer-assisted proofs through fourteen runners, not a general solution. The sandwich proves an exact finite rational search for each fixed speed vector, preserving equality at the threshold.
formal_statement: theorem P085 (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k) (v : Fin k → ℤ) (hv : ∀ i, v i ≠ 0) : ∃ t : ℝ, ∀ i, (1 : ℝ) / (k + 1) ≤ ‖((t * v i : ℝ) : UnitAddCircle)‖

name: Rainbow Trees in Subgraphs of Hypercubes
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C05 Trees
informal_statement_summary: Let G be a nonempty finite simple graph isomorphic to a (not necessarily induced) subgraph of an n-dimensional hypercube. Give its edges a proper colouring: edges sharing a vertex have distinct colours. Then every finite tree T with at most δ(G) edges has a rainbow copy in G, meaning an injective edge-preserving vertex map under which distinct edges of T receive distinct colours. Here δ(G) is the minimum degree. This is Theorem 1.2 of Crawford–Sankar–Schildkraut–Spiro, Rainbow Trees in Hypercubes (2025). In particular, every proper edge-colouring of Q_n contains every tree with at most n edges as a rainbow copy. P014 concerns the absence of rainbow cycles in the coordinate colouring; this is a different result. The Lean benchmark statement is registered; its full proof and substantive sandwich remain to be formalized.
formal_statement: theorem P086 {V W C : Type*} [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] [Fintype W] (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (ι : G →g H n) (hι : Injective ι) (c : G.lineGraph.Coloring C) (T : SimpleGraph W) [DecidableRel T.Adj] (hT : T.IsTree) (hsize : T.edgeFinset.card ≤ G.minDegree) : ∃ f : T →g G, Injective f ∧ Injective (c ∘ f.mapEdgeSet)

name: Galvin's Bipartite List-Edge-Colouring Theorem
difficulty: Calibration (upper-end; proved in literature; Lean proof pending)
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: Let M be a finite loopless bipartite multigraph, with parallel edges retained as distinct edge objects. Suppose every vertex is incident with at most d edges. For each edge e, choose a finite list L(e) of at least d allowed colours from an arbitrary common palette. Galvin's theorem asserts that one can select a colour c(e) from every list so that any two distinct edges with a common endpoint have different colours. No positivity condition on d is needed: the empty-edge case is included. The formal statement uses two-colourability of the underlying simple graph for bipartiteness, an explicit loop exclusion, and injectivity on incident edge sets for properness. This is a proved theorem and an upper-end calibration target, not an open list-colouring conjecture. Its full Lean proof is pending. A proven reduction derives Dinitz's theorem on choosing representatives from an n-by-n array of lists, distinct in each row and column.
formal_statement: theorem P087 {V E C : Type*} [Finite V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (d : ℕ) (M : Multigraph V E) (hloop : ∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) (hbi : M.toSimpleGraph.Colorable 2) (hdegree : ∀ v, (M.incidenceFinset v).card ≤ d) (L : E → Finset C) (hL : ∀ e, d ≤ (L e).card) : ∃ c : E → C, (∀ e, c e ∈ L e) ∧ ∀ v, Set.InjOn c ↑(M.incidenceFinset v)

name: Elementary Ramsey Binomial Bound
msc: 05C55 Generalized Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: For positive integers r and s, every finite simple graph with at least choose(r+s−2,r−1) vertices contains a clique of size r or an independent set of size s. This is the classical Erdős–Szekeres binomial upper bound for two-colour Ramsey numbers, not P003's modern exponential improvement. The full reference Lean proof is supplied: induction on the two target sizes splits the remaining vertices into neighbours and non-neighbours of one vertex and uses Pascal's identity. This is an elementary solved calibration problem. The benchmark file retains its exercise placeholder; the reference proof is kept separately.
formal_statement: theorem P088 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (r s : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r) (hs : 1 ≤ s) (h : (r + s - 2).choose (r - 1) ≤ Fintype.card V) : (∃ t : Finset V, G.IsNClique r t) ∨ ∃ t : Finset V, Gᶜ.IsNClique s t

name: Erdős–Szekeres Monotone Subsequence Theorem
msc: 05D10 Ramsey theory; 06A05 Total order
informal_statement_summary: For positive integers r and s, any sequence of n distinct elements of a linear order with n > (r−1)(s−1) has a strictly increasing subsequence of length r or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length s. Subsequences preserve the original index order and need not be contiguous. This is the classical Erdős–Szekeres theorem, stated over an arbitrary linear order rather than only the real numbers. A complete reference Lean proof assigns each position the lengths of its longest increasing and decreasing subsequences and applies the pigeonhole principle. The central benchmark keeps its exercise placeholder; the independent solution is provided separately as an elementary calibration reference.
formal_statement: theorem P089 {α : Type*} [LinearOrder α] (r s n : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r) (hs : 1 ≤ s) (hn : (r - 1) * (s - 1) < n) (a : Fin n → α) (ha : Function.Injective a) : (∃ f : Fin r ↪o Fin n, StrictMono (a ∘ f)) ∨ ∃ f : Fin s ↪o Fin n, StrictAnti (a ∘ f)

name: Restricted Eigenvalues of Strongly Regular Graphs
msc: 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra (matrices, eigenvalues, etc.); 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 90: Restricted eigenvalues of strongly regular graphs}
A finite simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is \emph{strongly regular} with
parameters $(n,k,\lambda,\mu)$ if it is $k$-regular, any two adjacent vertices
have exactly $\lambda$ common neighbours, and any two distinct non-adjacent
vertices have exactly $\mu$ common neighbours. Let $A$ be its adjacency matrix
over $\mathbb R$.
\begin{theorem}
If $Av=xv$ for a nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb R^{V(G)}$ whose coordinates sum to
zero, then
\[
x^2+(\mu-\lambda)x+(\mu-k)=0.
\]
\end{theorem}
Hence the eigenvalues of $A$ other than $k$ are the roots
$\tfrac12\bigl(\lambda-\mu\pm\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^2+4(k-\mu)}\bigr)$
\cite{Bose1963StronglyRegular,BrouwerHaemers2012Spectra,GodsilRoyle2001AGT}.

The formal statement uses Mathlib's \texttt{IsSRGWith} (with $\ell$ for
$\lambda$) and \texttt{adjMatrix}. The eigenvector is an arbitrary nonzero real
vector orthogonal to the all-ones vector, so no spectral theorem is needed.

\begin{thebibliography}{3}
\bibitem{Bose1963StronglyRegular}
R. C. Bose. \emph{Strongly regular graphs, partial geometries and partially
balanced designs}. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 13 (1963), 389--419.
\bibitem{BrouwerHaemers2012Spectra}
A. E. Brouwer, W. H. Haemers. \emph{Spectra of Graphs}. Universitext,
Springer, New York, 2012.
\bibitem{GodsilRoyle2001AGT}
C. Godsil, G. Royle. \emph{Algebraic Graph Theory}. Graduate Texts in
Mathematics 207, Springer, New York, 2001.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: A strongly regular graph with parameters (n, k, λ, μ) is k-regular on n vertices, with exactly λ common neighbours for adjacent pairs and μ for distinct non-adjacent pairs. Let A be its real adjacency matrix. If Av = xv for a nonzero vector v whose coordinates sum to zero, then x² + (μ − λ)x + (μ − k) = 0, so the eigenvalues other than k are the two roots of this quadratic. This is a classical calibration problem in algebraic graph theory. The formal statement uses Mathlib's IsSRGWith and adjMatrix with an arbitrary eigenvector orthogonal to the all-ones vector, so no spectral theorem is needed.

name: Bollobás's Uniform Set-Pairs Inequality
msc: 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 91: Bollobás's uniform set-pairs inequality}
Let $I$ be a finite index set, let $r,s\geq 0$, and let $A_i,B_i$ be finite
subsets of an arbitrary common universe, for $i\in I$.
\begin{theorem}[Bollobás]
If $|A_i|=r$, $|B_i|=s$ and $A_i\cap B_i=\varnothing$ for every $i$, and
$A_i\cap B_j\ne\varnothing$ for every ordered pair of distinct indices $i,j$,
then
\[
|I|\leq \binom{r+s}{r}.
\]
\end{theorem}
The cross-intersection condition is imposed in both directions, not just
for $i<j$. No assumption says that the unions $A_i\cup B_i$ coincide.
Only the index type is required to be finite in Lean; each individual set
is represented by a \texttt{Finset}. Disjointness expresses empty intersection,
and its negation expresses nonempty intersection without a decidable-equality
assumption in the public interface.

The bound is attained by all pairs $(A,X\setminus A)$ where $|X|=r+s$ and $|A|=r$.
If either size is zero, there can be at most one indexed pair. An empty family
is allowed.

\begin{thebibliography}{2}
\bibitem{Bollobas1965GeneralizedGraphs}
B. Bollobás. \emph{On generalized graphs}. Acta Mathematica Academiae
Scientiarum Hungaricae 16 (1965), 447--452.
\bibitem{Alon1985ExtremalSets}
N. Alon. \emph{An extremal problem for sets with applications to graph theory}.
Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 40 (1985), 82--89.
Corollary 1.2 with one ground part is the two-sided set-pairs theorem,
attributed there to Bollobás.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: Let (A_i,B_i) be a finite indexed family of pairs of finite sets, with every A_i having r elements and every B_i having s elements. Suppose A_i and B_i are disjoint, whereas A_i and B_j intersect whenever i≠j. Then there are at most choose(r+s,r) pairs. The ambient universe is arbitrary and need not have r+s elements; different pairs may have different unions. The empty family and zero sizes are included. Complementary pairs on a fixed (r+s)-element set attain the bound. A complete reference Lean proof establishes the stronger weighted set-pairs inequality by finite induction, implementing the first-element recurrence behind the permutation-events proof without measure theory.
formal_statement: theorem P091 {ι α : Type*} [Fintype ι] (r s : ℕ) (A B : ι → Finset α) (hA : ∀ i, (A i).card = r) (hB : ∀ i, (B i).card = s) (hdis : ∀ i, Disjoint (A i) (B i)) (hcross : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → ¬ Disjoint (A i) (B j)) : Fintype.card ι ≤ (r + s).choose r

formal_statement: theorem P107 (d : forall n : Nat, DegreeSequence n) (hgraph : forall n, (d n).IsGraphical) (hJ : Tendsto (fun n => ((d n).topDegreeSum : Real) / ((d n).total : Real)) atTop (𝓝 0)) (hδ : Tendsto (fun n => ((d n).minDegree : Real) / Real.log (n : Real)) atTop atTop) : ∃ ε : Nat -> Real, (forall n, ε n ∈ Set.Icc (0 : Real) 1) ∧ Tendsto ε atTop (𝓝 0) ∧ ∃ κ : forall n, Coupling (independentEdgeGraph n ((1 - ε n) • (d n).edgeMatrix.map poissonize)) (uniformDegreeGraph n (d n)), Tendsto (fun n => (κ n).embedProb) atTop (𝓝 1)

name: Hamiltonian Cycles in the Semi-Random Graph Process in Fewer than 2n Rounds (Frieze–Gao–MacRury–Prałat–Sorkin, Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C80 Random graphs; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Frieze, Gao, MacRury, Pralat and Sorkin (2023): the Hamiltonian-cycle constant of the semi-random graph process satisfies C_HAM <= 1.81701: for every q < 1 and epsilon > 0 and all large n, some online strategy builds a Hamiltonian cycle on [n] with probability at least q within (1.81701 + epsilon) n rounds. The constant is the numerical solution of the paper's differential equations for the DegreeGreedy, FullyRandomized and clean-up phases.
formal_statement: theorem P108 : roundConstant hamiltonianProperty ≤ 1.81701
